text: Green turtles live in tropical and subtropical waters worldwide. Adults commonly forage in shallow coastal seagrass beds and other nearshore waters.

IUCN global status: Least Concern (2025 assessment). The total number of wild green turtles has not been reliably counted; the assessment reports an increasing population trend but no global mature-individual total.
Green turtles may live for at least 70 years.
Loggerheads use open-ocean waters as juveniles and coastal and oceanic habitats as they grow; adults often feed in coastal waters and nest on sandy beaches.

IUCN global status: Vulnerable (assessed 2015). A reliable global headcount is unavailable; NOAA reports about 500 female loggerheads nest each year in the South Pacific, a regional nesting estimate rather than the total wild population.
Loggerheads can live for 80 years or more.
Leatherbacks travel through oceanic and coastal waters worldwide, including cooler waters, and nest on tropical and subtropical beaches.
IUCN global status: Vulnerable (assessed 2013). No reliable global headcount is available; NOAA estimates the global population declined about 40% over the past three generations.
Leatherback lifespan is uncertain; estimates suggest 45 to 50 years or more.
Hawksbills mainly live in warm nearshore waters, especially coral reefs, but also use mangrove estuaries, rocky areas, and open-ocean habitat when young.

IUCN global status: Critically Endangered (assessed 2008). A reliable global headcount is unavailable; NOAA reports around 6,000 to 8,000 hawksbills nest annually near Australia's Great Barrier Reef, a regional nesting estimate.
Hawksbills are estimated to live around 50 to 60 years, although their life expectancy has not been confirmed.
Kemp's ridleys mainly live in the Gulf of Mexico and nearby Atlantic waters. Adults forage in shallow coastal areas over sandy or muddy bottoms.
IUCN global status: Critically Endangered (assessed 2019). The IUCN estimate is 22,341 mature individuals; this counts mature turtles, not all ages, and is not a live census.
Kemp's ridleys are estimated to live at least 30 years, but their exact lifespan is not known.
Olive ridleys are found in tropical waters of the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans. They mostly live in the open ocean but also use coastal waters.

IUCN global status: Vulnerable (assessed 2008). A reliable global headcount is unavailable; NOAA estimates around 450,000 nesting females at La Escobilla, Mexico, a single-site estimate rather than the total wild population.
The exact lifespan of olive ridleys is not known, but they are thought to live for decades.
Flatback turtles live in shallow coastal waters around northern Australia and nearby regions, often over soft seabeds; they nest on Australian beaches.
IUCN global status: Data Deficient (assessed 1996). This means there is not enough information to determine its extinction risk; the assessment provides no global mature-individual count.
The IUCN assessment does not give a life-expectancy estimate for flatback turtles, so their lifespan is listed as unknown.
